To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we developed an experimental approach for generating and expanding anti-tumor CTL, suitable for adoptive immunotherapies.
we developed a procedure for generating anti‐tumor T cell lines from patients and their HLA identical sibling.

we have developed a novel method to generate anti‐tumor T‐cell clones from the peripheral blood of cancer patients and their HLA‐matched siblings, which are suitable for use in adoptive immunotherapy.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the immune system, and in particular the cellular immune response, in patients with cancer.
the development of a novel procedure to generate and expand anti‐tumor T‐cell lines from patients with cancer or their HLA identical sibling.
the development and characterization of new immunotherapeutic approaches for the treatment of patients affected by cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of the DC‐based approach for the generation of CTL‐lines is a promising strategy to obtain anti‐tumor T cell lines that could be used in adoptive immunotherapy approaches.
this is a very interesting and promising approach to the generation of anti-tumor cytotoxic T cells for adoptive therapy.

, in the present study, we have developed an efficient method to generate and expand anti‐tumor T cell clones from patients or their sibling donors, which are able to recognize autologous or allogeneic tumor cells and to kill them.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the use of autologous DC‐derived from the patients themselves and their HLA‐matched sibling donors, in combination with autologous or allogeneic PBMC, is suitable for the generation of anti‐tumoral cytotoxic T‐cells (CTL) lines.

we have shown that the use of dendritic cells and autologous peripheral blood mononucleated cells from patients with cancer is a suitable approach to obtain in vitro anti‐solid tumor cytotoxic T‐lymphocytes, that can be used for adoptative immunotherapy.
our experimental approach was able to generate anti‐tumor T cell lines that could be potentially used in adoptive immunotherapy protocols.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is feasible to generate and expand anti-tumor CTL in vitro using both autologous or allogeneic HLA‐identic sibling PBMC and DC as source of tumor antigens.
it is possible to expand tumor‐reactive T‐cells ex‐vivo, even from a single donor, in a relatively short period of time.
we have developed an ex vivo method to generate anti‐tumor T‐cell lines from the peripheral blood of patients with cancer.
